client: I've been really anxious about this weekend because my partner wants me to meet their friends for the first time, and I just can't stop thinking about it. I keep imagining all these scenarios where they don't like me or think I'm not good enough for my partner. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to help much, because the anxiety just feels so real and so big.
therapist: It sounds like your mind has been working overtime, running through all these "what if" scenarios, and that kind of anticipatory anxiety can feel completely overwhelming and very real. I also notice that even as you're describing something that feels so big and scary, there's a part of you that showed up here today anyway — and that takes courage. I'm curious, when you imagine these friends not approving of you, what does that say about you in those moments — what's the deeper fear underneath that thought?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I guess... when I picture them judging me or pulling away, it feels like it confirms something I already believe about myself — that I'm just too much, or maybe not enough, I can never quite figure out which one. Like there's this voice that says if these people really knew me, they'd realize I don't actually belong in the group. It's embarrassing to even say out loud, but that fear of being truly seen and then rejected is probably what keeps me from just relaxing and enjoying time with them.
therapist: What you just shared takes real vulnerability, and that fear of being "too much" or "not enough" — sometimes both at once — is such a painful place to live from. That voice you're describing sounds like it's been around for a while, quietly shaping how safe it feels to let people in. I'm wondering, is this the first time you've named that fear out loud, and what's it like to hear yourself say it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, I think it might be the first time I've actually said it out loud like that, and it feels kind of strange — like I've been carrying this thing around forever and suddenly it has a name. There's a part of me that feels a little relieved, but there's also this other part that's kind of embarrassed, like I shouldn't need to be in a room talking about this. I guess I always figured if I just kept pushing through, it would eventually stop mattering so much.
therapist: There's something really meaningful about this moment — giving a name to something you've carried quietly for so long, and still showing up even when part of you says you shouldn't have to. That belief that you should just "push through" is worth gently questioning, because it sounds like it's kept you from getting the relief you're feeling just a little of right now. What do you think that part of you was trying to protect you from, by keeping this unnamed for so long?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I think that part of me was trying to protect me from... looking weak, maybe? Like if I named it, if I actually admitted I was struggling with the loneliness and the anxiety, then it would become real and I'd have to face the fact that I can't just handle things on my own like I always told myself I could. It's a strange feeling to sit with — like there's a tiny bit of relief here, but also this nagging voice saying "you're making too big a deal out of this."
therapist: That voice telling you you're "making too big a deal out of this" — that's the same protector, still working hard to keep you from fully landing here. And yet the relief you're feeling is real data too, worth trusting just as much as that critical voice. I'm curious — if a close friend told you what you just told me, would you tell them they were making too big a deal out of it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, no, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably listen and tell them their feelings made sense. But it feels different when it's me, like I don't have the same... permission, I guess, to take up that kind of space.
therapist: That word — *permission* — really stands out, because it points to something important: somewhere along the way, you learned that your struggles needed to earn their place, that you had to justify taking up space even in your own inner world. And there's something quietly tender in the way you said that, like part of you recognizes the unfairness of that double standard even as another part still holds onto it. Where do you think you first learned that your needs required that kind of permission?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I think it probably started with my family, honestly. Growing up, there was always this unspoken rule that you didn't make a fuss, that other people's problems were more serious than yours, and if you brought something up you'd better have a good reason for it. I guess I internalized that so deeply that now I'm the one doing it to myself, and it feels almost automatic, like I don't even question it until someone points it out like you just did.
therapist: What you just described — that unspoken family rule — sounds like it became the blueprint for how you relate to your own needs, and it makes so much sense that it feels automatic now, because you learned it before you even had words for it. It's really significant that you can see it so clearly in this moment, because awareness like that is often where change begins to take root. I'm curious, now that you can name where it came from, does it feel any different — like it has a little less power over you, or does it still feel just as heavy?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I want to say it feels lighter, but I'm not sure it actually does yet. Like, understanding where it came from doesn't automatically make me stop feeling guilty when I put myself first — my chest still tightens the same way when I think about telling my family I need something. It's almost frustrating, because I thought naming it would feel more like a relief than it does.
therapist: That frustration makes complete sense, and it's actually a really important truth about this work — insight is the beginning, not the finish line, and your nervous system has been practicing that guilt response for a very long time. I notice there's something almost urgent in the way you're describing this, like a part of you is disappointed in yourself for not feeling better faster — which, if you think about it, is that same old rule showing up again, telling you you're not doing this right either. What would it mean to give yourself the same patience you'd offer that friend — to let this be a slow unfolding rather than something you have to get right immediately?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Yeah, I hear what you're saying, and part of me knows you're right — but it's almost like even trying to be patient with myself feels like another thing I could fail at. Like, what if I'm just using "being gentle with myself" as an excuse to not actually change? I guess I'm scared that if I stop pushing so hard, I'll just stay stuck in this guilt forever.
therapist: That fear — that self-compassion is just a disguise for staying stuck — is such a common trap, and it's worth gently challenging, because pushing harder hasn't dissolved the guilt yet, has it? Self-compassion isn't the opposite of change; it's actually what makes change feel safe enough to sustain. I'm curious, in your experience, have you ever grown or shifted in a meaningful way because you were hard on yourself — or did it tend to happen in moments when you finally felt safe enough to breathe?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Honestly, when you put it that way, I have to admit that most of the times I actually changed something meaningful, it wasn't because I beat myself up enough. It was more like... when I finally stopped fighting so hard and just let myself sit with something. But I'm still not fully convinced, because it feels like if I give myself too much grace about the loneliness and the way I've pulled away from people, I'll just keep doing it and calling it "self-compassion."
therapist: You just gave yourself some really important evidence there — that real change has come from softening, not from pushing, and that's worth holding onto. And I think the distinction you're reaching for is actually a wise one: self-compassion isn't about excusing the pulling away, it's about understanding it clearly enough that you don't need to keep doing it. What do you think the loneliness and pulling away has been trying to do for you — what has it been protecting you from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That question kind of stops me in my tracks, because I haven't really thought about it that way before — like the loneliness was doing something for me, not just happening to me. I think... maybe it's been protecting me from the risk of being really seen and then rejected anyway, like if I pull away first, at least I'm in control of the distance. But saying that out loud makes me feel kind of sad, because it means I've been the one keeping people out while also feeling alone.
therapist: What you just uncovered is profound — that the loneliness wasn't something happening *to* you, but something you've been quietly orchestrating to stay safe, and recognizing that takes real courage. That sadness you're feeling right now makes complete sense, because you're grieving something — all the connection that fear of rejection has cost you. And I want to gently reflect that the fact you can feel that sadness, rather than just pushing past it, might be the very first step toward choosing something different.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech
